title: Kyiv's baptism (988)
hookLine: Prince Vladimir's people are baptized in the Dnieper, a shared root of Orthodox and Eastern Catholics

cards: A wide river runs past a city on high bluffs. On the bank stand priests in vestments, come from the Greek lands to the south.

Into the water walk the people of Kyiv, the old chronicle says, some up to their necks, some to their chests, the young ones near the shore, parents holding their babies. The priests stand and say the prayers over them.
A whole city, baptized together in the Dnieper. Today, Kyiv's baptism.

teach.b: Our main source is the old chronicle of Kyiv, written by monks, sometimes called the Tale of Bygone Years. It tells the story of Vladimir, grand prince of Kyiv.
His envoys, it says, came back from a liturgy in the great church of Constantinople and said they hadn't known whether they were in heaven or on earth, only that God dwells there among people.
The beauty of the worship moved them.
Vladimir himself was baptized, married a sister of the emperors in Constantinople, and came home with priests.
Then he sent word through the city: anyone, rich or poor, who did not come to the river would be counted the prince's enemy.
That was a command, not an invitation, and it's worth hearing honestly, the day after Charlemagne. The chronicle says the people came gladly.
Whatever was in each heart, they came, and the chronicle tells the scene with real tenderness: people standing in the water, the priests praying, and Vladimir glad that he and his people knew God.
This baptism is a shared root.
Orthodox churches of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus trace their faith to that river, and so does the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, which prays in the Eastern way and is in communion with Rome.
Both remember Vladimir as a saint. One river, two families who each call it the beginning. The Gospels use the same Greek word, baptizo, when Jesus sends the apostles out to baptize all nations.
A people's faith beginning not in a building, but in water, out under the sky.

how: Orthodox Christians and Ukrainian Greek Catholics both keep a feast of Saint Vladimir and remember the baptism of Kyiv; Catholics of the Latin rite join in praying for Ukraine and for unity among Christians.

games.q: you're Vladimir, newly baptized, home with priests from Constantinople. how do you bring the faith to your city?
o: send word for everyone to come to the river.
build a church first and wait.
games.why: the chronicle says he sent word through the city, and the people walked into the Dnieper while the priests prayed.

practice: Let your breath move slowly, like water past a bank, and with each breath out, think of one person in Ukraine you will never meet: someone waking up there today, someone far from home.
If you pray, ask God's peace and protection for everyone who lives there, in your own words or with an Our Father; if you don't, simply hold them in mind, one breath at a time.

wordCard.voice: Kyiv's baptism. Prince Vladimir's people baptized in the Dnieper, a root shared by Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to dip, to immerse — the Gospels' word for baptizing, and a fair picture of a city in a river.

carryVoice: Your line: baptized in the river. Water, prayers, and a whole city at the shore. Until tomorrow.
